archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A Jacksonville side that wins on a top-five passing offense and a run defense that shuts the ground game down, while a leaky deep secondary and an injured line keep it a tier below the true heavyweights.

report.headline: Offense got better, defense got worse, and the record is honest this time.
report.take:
Last year's 13-4 Jaguars were a good team riding a lot of luck: they led the league in wins over expected (3.87) and in cover rate. This year's 4-2 team is built differently. The efficiency is about the same, with net EPA fourth in the league, but the luck is gone. Wins over expected sits at 0.44, and the point differential implies 3.6 wins, so the record is earned. The bigger change is where the efficiency comes from. In Liam Coen's second year the offense has jumped from 13th in EPA per play to 5th, carried by a passing game that ranks 4th (0.221 EPA per dropback). Meanwhile a defense that was 5th in EPA allowed last year has slipped to 17th.

The passing attack is the engine, and it is spread out. Parker Washington leads the team in targets, Brenton Strange is a real second option at tight end, and Jakobi Meyers and Brian Thomas Jr. fill out the room. Trevor Lawrence has started every game, and his last two have been his best through the air: 331 yards against Philadelphia and 306 against Houston, each worth double-digit passing EPA. The run game around him is efficient rather than explosive. Bhayshul Tuten takes most of the carries and the team ranks 6th in run EPA and 3rd in short-yardage conversion. Ball security helps too, at +5 in turnover differential.

The 17.3 points allowed per game (3rd) flatters the defense. Yardage allowed ranks 21st and EPA allowed 17th. What keeps the scoreboard clean is a 40% red-zone touchdown rate allowed (3rd) and nine takeaways, and both tend to drift toward the middle. The shape of the defense is clear. It is elite against the run (5th in rush EPA allowed, 3rd in explosive runs allowed) and the best in the league on short throws. It is 28th on deep passes and 29th in EPA allowed to opposing WR1s. Offenses have noticed: they pass against Jacksonville more than almost anyone (the 2nd-strongest pass funnel). Cincinnati threw for 428 yards in Week 4 and Houston for 312 in the Week 6 loss.

From here the schedule is kind. There are two games with 1-5 Tennessee, and Houston, Indianapolis, Dallas and Washington all have losing records. The Jaguars already hold a clear AFC South lead. The questions are depth and health. Right tackle Anton Harrison, a 92%-snap starter, is on IR after knee surgery with a recovery range that runs from weeks to months. The secondary that already gives up the big play has a questionable safety and an injured corner. This looks like a playoff team, and a contender only if the deep pass defense tightens.

strengths.title: A top-five passing offense
strengths.body: Jacksonville's dropbacks rank 4th in EPA. The production is spread across a WR1 in Washington, a featured tight end and two veteran wideouts, so no single coverage takes it away. It has trended up, with the two best passing EPA games coming in the last two weeks, and it gives up sacks at a low rate despite a slow time to throw. With the same starting quarterback every week and a deep target tree, this should hold up. Harrison's absence at tackle is the main threat to it.

strengths.title: Run defense that erases the ground game
strengths.body: The front ranks 5th in rush EPA allowed and 3rd in explosive runs allowed. Cincinnati managed 23 rushing yards and Philadelphia 22. The underneath coverage is also the stingiest in the league on short passes. This holds up because it is structural, but it is also why opponents pass so often against this defense.

strengths.title: Winning the turnover margin
strengths.body: The Jaguars have nine takeaways against four giveaways, 6th in turnover margin per game, after ranking 3rd in the same stat last year. A second straight season near the top suggests a real habit (a careful quarterback and an opportunistic defense) rather than pure bounces. Expect the margin to stay positive, though probably smaller.

concerns.title: The deep secondary is getting beaten
concerns.body: This defense ranks 28th in EPA allowed on deep throws and 29th against opposing WR1s. Offenses are steering into it, which is why Cincinnati and Houston both threw for 300-plus yards. This is a real flaw, not just the cost of the strong run defense. It gets more dangerous with safety Antonio Johnson (86% of snaps) questionable and corner Montaric Brown out.

concerns.title: Points allowed are ahead of the defense
concerns.body: A defense that ranks 3rd in points allowed but 21st in yards allowed and 17th in EPA is leaning on a 40% red-zone touchdown rate and timely takeaways. Both usually move back toward league average. Expect more of those red-zone trips to end in touchdowns, and the points-allowed number to rise toward the middle of the league.

concerns.title: Line strain and penalties
concerns.body: Backs get just 1.85 yards before contact (28th), and Lawrence holds the ball longer than most. The line now loses a 92%-snap starting tackle for a stretch that could last weeks or months. Penalties are piling up too: 125 yards in the Cincinnati win and 412 on the season. A thinner line plus flags is how drives die.

trend.note: The passing offense has peaked in the last two games while the pass defense has sprung leaks: 428 yards allowed in Cincinnati and 312 in the Houston shootout loss. The two trends have roughly offset each other.

nextGame.headline: Rested Jaguars host a turnover-prone Colts team in the division
nextGame.body:
Jacksonville comes off its bye with 14 days of rest to host a 2-4 Indianapolis team that ranks 26th in net EPA. No line has been posted by the Book yet. The matchup turns on a strength-on-strength fight. The Colts' offense is built on the run (2nd in rush EPA) and is poor through the air (28th in pass EPA), and Jacksonville's front is 5th in rush EPA allowed. On the other side, Indianapolis's defense is 31st against the run, generates little pressure (26th) and has only three takeaways. That combination suits a Jaguars offense that protects the ball and can lean on Tuten. The one real Colts strength on defense is third downs, where they allow conversions at the 4th-lowest rate.

Availability favors Jacksonville. Cornerback Sauce Gardner (89% of snaps) was doubtful with a week-to-week calf strain. Edge rusher Arden Key is on IR into November. Tight end Tyler Warren (91% of snaps) and linebacker Jaylon Carlies were out as of the last report, with return estimates before this game that are not promises. Alec Pierce's heel kept him on IR. The Jaguars have their own holes: Harrison is out at tackle, Brown is out at corner, safety Johnson is questionable with an ankle, and long snapper Ross Matiscik is out.

waysToWin.title: Feed Tuten against a soft run defense
waysToWin.body: Indianapolis is 31st in rush EPA allowed, and opposing lead backs have outscored their usual output against it by more than any other defense allows. Jacksonville's efficient, short-yardage-strong run game can stay on schedule. That keeps Lawrence out of obvious passing downs, where the Colts' third-down defense is at its best.

waysToWin.title: Stop the run, make Jones throw
waysToWin.body: The Colts' offense works only on the ground. If Jacksonville's top-five run defense wins that matchup, Indianapolis has to pass, and its passing game ranks 28th in EPA. Forcing the Colts into long down-and-distance plays to the Jaguars' best trait.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover battle again
waysToWin.body: Indianapolis has the league's worst turnover margin and has forced just three takeaways. Jacksonville has been plus-five. Steady ball security against a defense that rarely takes the ball away tilts possessions toward the Jaguars.

waysToLose.title: Colts grind the clock on the ground
waysToLose.body: Indianapolis is 4th in time of possession and 2nd in rush EPA. If its run game wins early downs, it can shorten the game and keep Jacksonville's passing attack on the sideline. That turns a game the Jaguars should control into a coin flip.

waysToLose.title: Drives stall on third down and flags
waysToLose.body: The Colts allow third-down conversions at the 4th-lowest rate and are the league's least-penalized team. Jacksonville averages 7.7 penalties a game and is missing its starting right tackle. Self-inflicted second-and-longs feed straight into the one thing this Colts defense does well.

waysToLose.title: Shots over a depleted secondary
waysToLose.body: Even a weak passing offense can hit a defense that ranks 28th on deep throws, and Jacksonville may be without both Brown and Johnson. Houston showed how fast a Jaguars lead can turn into a shootout loss once the deep ball starts landing.

nextGame.watch: Watch Jacksonville's run defense against the Colts' ground game on early downs. If Daniel Jones faces third-and-long, this game tilts heavily to the Jaguars.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying team is a legitimate top-five unit by net EPA, and the record matches it. Unlike last year, there is no big pile of close-game luck waiting to regress. The passing offense and the run defense look structural, and the schedule is one of the softer paths left. It includes two games against Tennessee's 31st-ranked offense and several sub-.500 opponents, with Baltimore, Chicago and Pittsburgh the real tests. That points to winning the AFC South.

Two things should regress. The red-zone defense and takeaway pace are propping up points allowed, so expect that number to climb toward the low 20s. The deep-pass problem will keep producing shootouts against good passing teams. The offense's ceiling depends on how long Harrison is out. The 3-to-5-week end of his range barely dents the season, while the 3-to-4-month end puts real pressure on a line that already grades poorly on yards before contact.
swingFactors: Anton Harrison's surgery outcome and return timing
Health of the secondary (Johnson, Brown) against the deep ball
How much the red-zone defense regresses

confidence.note: Six games; the efficiency backs the record, but the defensive ranks are unstable and the OT injury timeline is wide open.
